1:
Why the prophet had to be woken gets two very different treatments. Henry takes it at face value, that in the middle of a conference with an angel on matters of public concern he grew dull and fell asleep; his spirit was willing and his flesh weak, and either the strangeness of the visions stupefied him or their sweetness composed him. He draws from it that we need the Spirit of God not only to make divine things known but to make us notice them. Ellicott suspects the appearance rather than the sleep: the phrase may mean the angel woke him again, or the angel may have gone out for fresh instruction from a higher one and returned; and it may be either that the prophet fell into a lethargy between visions or that all these visions are seen in a dream and he only seemed within it to be woken.

How far the candlestick answers the one in the sanctuary is the question, and the differences are counted differently. Clarke says it is formed in some measure after that one, but the earlier had neither bowl nor pipes nor the two trees. Keil and Delitzsch call it unquestionably a figure of the seven-branched candlestick and list what is peculiar to this one: the oil vessel at the top, which the earlier lacked since its lamps were filled by the priests, and the pipes conducting the oil, the earlier having only arms for the lamps.

How many pipes there were is disputed, and the answers range widely. Wesley takes them at seven, each lamp having one pipe reaching to the bowl; Clarke assumes the same, the trees supplying the bowl, the bowl the pipes, the pipes the lamps. Keil and Delitzsch report the question as open, whether the repeated numeral means seven and seven, that is fourteen, or something else. Ellicott renders it seven pipes apiece and so arrives at forty-nine, remarking that since the candlestick is only visionary we need not trouble about its construction, and that a great number is named to indicate an unlimited supply of oil. He records and rejects two alternatives, one making the two sevens serve different offices and the other cancelling a numeral, calling such emendations arbitrary; Calvin meets the same question at the cruses, reporting the view that there were seven to each lamp but approving rather that every lamp had one.

What it all means Calvin takes as the point of the vision, Clarke as an allegory to be resolved. Calvin says the explanation is added at once, God declaring that his Spirit was sufficient to preserve the church without earthly helps, so that his grace would always shine and could never be extinguished. He adds a defence of the old ceremony: the design was to show that the temple symbol was neither superfluous nor insignificant, so the Jews might know their labour in lighting those lamps was no deceptive spectacle but a real symbol of a favour to be exhibited at length.

Clarke offers a general sense and then a detailed one. Generally the candlestick and its furniture are an emblem of the pure service of God; or it may stand for the whole Jewish state, ecclesiastical and civil, the oil for the grace of God, and the two trees for the source of infinite love from which it proceeds. Then he sets out a scheme in five steps: the trees are the divine goodness yielding oil from the berry, a pipe from each conveys it to the bowl, the bowl is Christ the Mediator through whom all grace descends, the pipes are the means of grace, and the lamps the Spirit of God in his plenitude of gifts. Wesley keeps to one figure, the church made of pure gold to be a light in the world, burning with oil not pressed out by man but freely flowing from God.
4:
What the prophet's question covers Ellicott settles first: the word these does not refer merely to the two trees but to everything described. On the question put back to him, Gill offers two accounts, either that it upbraids his ignorance or, as he prefers, that it is meant to quicken his attention to the interpretation coming.

The word about might and power is where Clarke writes at greatest heat. He notes that the prince needed especial encouragement, then distinguishes the terms, might meaning strength of one's own and power authority derived from others, against which is set the energy of the Most High. From that he draws a rule and defends it against an objection he puts in the mouth of the world: no secular arm, no human prudence, no earthly policy and no suits at law shall ever be used for the founding or preservation of the church; and when the world answers that these are means we must have recourse to, since otherwise the cause of God may be ruined, he replies in three words that Satan lies. Wesley glosses the second term as courage and valour. Ellicott explains why a vision is called a word at all, being a symbolical prophecy, and adds what the building was for: the congregation the candlestick symbolised needed a sanctuary in which to let its light shine.

The great mountain is agreed to be opposition. Gill offers the men who obstructed the building or the Persian monarchy and its capital, a mountain being a symbol of a kingdom. Clarke names the royal prohibition that had stopped the work. Ellicott calls it figurative of the colossal difficulties raised by the neighbouring powers, and Wesley reduces it to all the opposers put together. On the levelling Ellicott notes that the original is singularly graphic and consists of a single word, literally to a plain, and that the ancient Greek mistook it for an Aramaic infinitive, rendering that the prince should bring the work to a successful issue.

The shout over the last stone is read as a prayer by three. Ellicott takes the crowning stone to stand for the whole building and the words to be a prayer in the form of a triumphal shout, that God's favour may rest on the house for ever. Clarke turns it into two exclamations, admiration of the structure and a wish that God's favour may rest on it.

The change of person in the next verse Ellicott explains two ways, either as the common Hebrew usage in addressing a nation regarded now as a corporate unity and now as a collection of individuals, or as an actual change of audience, the singular to the prince and the plural to the people. On the day of small things he treats the question as equivalent to a prohibition, since no one who intended great things ever despised such a day, and re-renders what follows, that these seven shall behold the plummet with joy and the eyes of the Lord sweep through the whole earth. Clarke supplies the taunt the verse answers, that these feeble Jews could do nothing, and replies that God will build by them and perfect it; he makes the seven either the particular providence of God or the ministering spirits employed in dispensing it. Wesley says God often chooses weak instruments for mighty things, and though the beginnings are small he can make the latter end greatly increase. Henry states the principle behind the passage: though the instruments be weak and unlikely God often chooses such, the dawning light is not to be despised since it will shine more and more to the perfect day, and all who have the plummet in their hands must look up to the eyes of the Lord. Keil and Delitzsch note only that this much gives the prophet the general meaning, one point remaining obscure to him.
11:
Twice the prophet asks, and the two askings are not identical. Henry makes the point deliberately: he first wanted to know what the two olive trees were, and afterwards what the two olive branches were, the boughs that hung over the bowl and distilled oil into it; and Henry draws from the change that when we enquire after the grace of God it must be as it is communicated by the fruitful boughs of word and ordinance, which is a revealed thing, rather than as it is resident in the tree where all the springs are, which is a secret thing. He adds that the first question got no reply at all, and that this is why it had to be renewed. Gill puts the same fact more plainly, that the second was asked before any answer to the former had come, being of the same import. Ellicott supplies a motive neither of them gives: the prophet was not yet satisfied why there should be two trees, since only the prince had so far been named and he could hardly be figured by a pair of them. Henry also notes the angel's method, that he obliged the prophet to own his ignorance expressly before he would inform him.

On what exactly was seen, Ellicott corrects the English. The word rendered branches is better bunches of olives, and two details enter the vision here for the first time, the cluster of fruit on each tree and the two golden spouts. He would render that the clusters rest in the two golden spouts which pour out from themselves the gold, the arrangement being a spout turned upward on each side of the bowl, into which the clusters emptied spontaneously, and from which the oil ran down into the bowl and thence through the forty-nine pipes to the lamps; the gold, he says, stands for pure bright oil. He rejects the received rendering through on grammatical grounds, the article being prefixed to the participle, and he records that the old Greek understood the gold as golden funnels rather than golden oil and turned the participle active, which pour into and lead up into the golden funnels. Clarke says only that they are boughs laden with olive berries. Wesley describes the fastening, a hole through the side of the bowl to let the oil run in, and reads the whole as an emblem of supernatural grace, branches filled from the true tree that are ever emptying themselves and ever full; and so, he says, are the gospel ordinances.

The answer divides the voices. Clarke takes the two sons of oil for Joshua and Zerubbabel, appointed by the Lord and standing by him, the one ministering in the ecclesiastical and the other in the civil state; and he is candid that the whole hieroglyphic may not be comprehensible, since the interpreting angel declined the prophet's questions about it. Ellicott agrees on the persons and adds the structure: the preceding vision assured the religious head that he was accepted and purified, this one assures the civil head of help in his work, and the two are named together because the nation's prosperity depends on their joint labour. Wesley takes them for Christ and the Holy Spirit, both sent by the Father and standing ready to go. Gill will not choose, canvassing the gifts and graces of the Spirit, then Christ and the Spirit, then Pemble's open query whether it be Christ and the Comforter, or Christ in his two natures, or Christ in his two offices, noting that the last was an ancient view since censured. Henry keeps both by making them conditional on what the candlestick is, the magistracy and ministry if it is the visible church, Christ and the Spirit if it is the church of the first-born. Delitzsch adds nothing here beyond the words of the questions and of the answer themselves.
